L240@P6-7: 7Chapter 1
L241@P7: Introduction
L242@P7: The main purpose of the pdfTEX project is to create and maintain an extension of TEX that
L243@P7: can produce PDF output directly from TEX source files and improve/enhance the result of TEX
L244@P7: typesetting with the help of PDF output. When PDF output is not selected, pdfTEX produces
L245@P7: standard DVI output. An important aspect of the project is to investigate alternative justification
L246@P7: algorithms; notably, the margin kerning and font expansion algorithms following the HZ microtypography algorithm by Prof. Hermann Zapf.
L247@P7: pdfTEX is maintained by Hàn Th´ê Thành, the original author, and others. The pdfTEX home
L248@P7: page is https://www.pdftex.org. Please send bug reports, suggestions, etc., to the mailing list
L249@P7: (https://lists.tug.org/pdftex).
L250@P7: pdfTEX is based on the original TEX sources and Web2C, and has been successfully compiled on
L251@P7: Unix, Windows and many other systems. It is actively maintained, with great care taken to keep
L252@P7: new pdfTEX versions backward-compatible with earlier ones.
L253@P7: A conservative successor to TEX, named ε-TEX, was developed in the 1990s. Since pdfTEX
L254@P7: version 1.40, the ε-TEX extensions are compiled as part of the pdfTEX engine and thus always
L255@P7: available. For documentation on the ε-TEX extensions, see https://ctan.org/pkg/etex.
L256@P7: Furthermore, pdfTEX itself has acquired plenty of extensions over the years which are not related
L257@P7: specifically to PDF output, generally new primitives for various features that are inconvenient or
L258@P7: impossible to implement at the TEX level. Many of these extensions have been adopted across all
L259@P7: engines (sometimes with different primitive names or variant functionality), and some are required
L260@P7: by LATEX. Therefore, in most distributions etex is a link to pdftex; the difference being whether
L261@P7: DVI or PDF output is generated by default.
L262@P7: Other extensions are mlTEX and encTEX; these are also included in the pdfTEX implementation,
L263@P7: although they are rarely used for new documents.
L264@P7: pdfTEX does not natively support UTF-8 input text, Unicode-encoded fonts, or anything else
L265@P7: related to Unicode, as it was written long before Unicode became widespread. Making those changes
L266@P7: to the engine now would necessarily create unacceptable incompatibilities, so there are no plans to
L267@P7: do so. Thus, when using pdfTEX, LATEX and other formats handle UTF-8 (and other) input at the
L268@P7: TEX macro level, which works well enough in practice for most documents. It is also possible to use
L269@P7: TrueType and OpenType fonts with pdfTEX, if you choose an 8-bit subset to be encoded.
L270@P7: If you need a TEX engine with native support for Unicode input, TrueType fonts, OpenType fonts, please look into LuaTEX (https://ctan.org/pkg/luatex) or XeTEX (https://tug.
L271@P7: org/xetex).

L2582@P69: Character translation: TCX
L2611@P70: This section describes the steps needed to get pdfTEX running on a system where pdfTEX is not yet
L2612@P70: installed. Nowadays all known TEX distributions, such as TEX Live, MiKTEX, and MacTEX, include
L2613@P70: pdfTEX already. For example, the TEX Live distribution comes with pdfTEX versions for many Unix,
L2614@P70: Windows, and Mac systems; more information can be found at https://tug.org/texlive. When
L2615@P70: you use any of these distributions, you don’t need to bother with the pdfTEX installation procedure
L2616@P70: in this chapter.
L2628@P70: Given a directory where the sources have been downloaded or checked out, some working on a Unix
L2629@P70: system the following steps are needed to compile pdfTEX:
L2630@P70: cd source # from branches/stable!
L2631@P70: ./build-pdftex.sh
L2632@P70: The binary pdftex will hopefully then end up in the subdirectory build-pdftex/texk/web2c.
L2633@P70: The additional utilities pdftosrc and ttf2afm are in the pdfTEX source repository, but are not
L2634@P70: built by default. If they are needed, edit build-pdftex.sh to --enable them.
L2635@P70: For pdfTEX maintainers: a sibling script to build-pdftex.sh is in the repository, namely
L2636@P70: sync-pdftex.sh, which syncs changes from a TEX Live source repository to a pdfTEX source repository. Read and understand the script before using it!
L2637@P70-71: 71A.3 Placing files
L2638@P71: The next step is to put the newly-compiled pdftex (and, if enabled, pdftosrc and/or ttf2afm)
L2639@P71: binaries into the installed distribution. E.g., for a typical TEX Live system:
L2640@P71: /usr/local/texlive/2026/bin/x86_64-linux, replacing x86_64-linux with the appropriate platform name. (As always, it is sensible to rename the installed pdftex binary first and not just
L2641@P71: overwrite it.)
L2642@P71: If you’re doing this into a live hierarchy, run fmtutil-sys refresh afterwards, so that all
L2643@P71: formats are regenerated system-wide with the new pdftex binary.
L2644@P71: If what you want is to test a new version of pdftex, and not replace the installed version, the
L2645@P71: best approach is to copy it into the binary directory as, say, pdftex.new. The different executable
L2646@P71: name can sometimes change the files found and other behavior, but usually this won’t matter.
L2647@P71: pdfTEX uses the Kpathsea library to search for supporting files; many variables and configuration
L2648@P71: files can come into play. See the Kpathsea manual: https://tug.org/kpathsea.
L2649@P71: A.4 Configuration of pdfTEX
L2650@P71: As opposed to TEX with its DVI output, the pdfTEX program does not have a separate postprocessing stage to transform the TEX input into final PDF. As a consequence, all data needed for building
L2651@P71: the PDF must be available during the pdfTEX run, in particular information on media dimensions
L2652@P71: and offsets, graphics files for embedding, and font information (font files, encodings).
L2653@P71: When TEX builds a page, it places items relative to the (1in,1in) offset from the top left page
L2654@P71: corner (the DVI reference point). Separate DVI postprocessors allow specifying the paper size (e.g.,
L2655@P71: A4 or letter), so that this reference point is moved to the correct position on the paper, and the
L2656@P71: text ends up at the right place.
L2657@P71: In PDF, the paper dimensions are part of the page definition, and pdfTEX therefore requires
L2658@P71: that they be defined at the beginning of the pdfTEX run. As with pages described by PostScript,
L2659@P71: the PDF reference point is in the lower left corner.
L2660@P71: Formerly, these dimensions and other pdfTEX parameters were read in from a configuration file
L2661@P71: named pdftex.cfg, which had a special (non-TEX) format, at the start of processing. Nowadays
L2662@P71: such a file is ignored by pdfTEX. Instead, the page dimensions and offsets, as well as many other
L2663@P71: parameters, can be set by pdfTEX primitives during the pdfTEX format building process, so that
L2664@P71: the settings are dumped into the fresh format and consequently will be used when pdfTEX is later
L2665@P71: called with that format. All settings from the format can still be overridden during a pdfTEX run
L2666@P71: by using the same primitives. This configuration concept is a more unified approach, as it avoids a
L2667@P71: configuration file with a special format.
L2668@P71: A list of pdfTEX primitives likely relevant to setting up the pdfTEX engine is given in the table
L2669@P71: below. All primitives are described in detail in previous sections.

L2735@P73: A.5 Creating format files
L2736@P73: The pdfTEX engine supports building separate formats for either DVI or PDF output in the same
L2737@P73: way as the classical TEX engine does for DVI. Format generation (and other initex features) is
L2738@P73: enabled by the -ini option. The default mode (DVI or PDF) can be chosen either on the command
L2739@P73: line by setting the option -output-format to dvi or pdf, or by setting the \pdfoutput parameter.
L2740@P73: The format file inherits this setting, so that a later invocation of pdfTEX with this format starts
L2741@P73: in the preselected mode (which can still be overridden). A format file can be read in only by the
L2742@P73: engine that has generated it; a format incompatible with an engine leads to a fatal error.
L2743@P73: It is customary to package the configuration and macro file input into a .ini file. E.g., the file
L2744@P73: etex.ini in figure A.2 is for generating an ε-TEX format with DVI output. It has been traditional
L2745@P73: for many years to generate etex.fmt with pdfTEX rather than the original ε-TEX, because pdfTEX
L2746@P73: contains useful additional programming and other non-PDF-related features.
L2747@P73: The pdfetex.ini file figure A.3 shows the corresponding format with PDF output by default;
L2748@P73: this is what creates the format file read when pdftex is normally invoked.
L2749@P73: The corresponding pdfTEX invocations for format generation are:
L2750@P73: pdftex -ini *etex.ini
L2751@P73: pdftex -ini *pdfetex.ini
L2752@P73: These calls produce format files etex.fmt, pdfetex.fmt, as the default format file name is taken
L2753@P73: from the input file name. You can override this with the -jobname option. The asterisk * before
L2754@P73: the file name is an unusual flag, only used in -ini mode, which causes the pdfTEX engine to enable
L2755@P73: ε-TEX’s features.
L2756@P73: To reiterate, the distribution (TEX Live, MiKTEX) usually takes care of format (re)generation.
L2757@P73: The above is if you need to do such things manually for testing, debugging, development, etc.
L2758@P73: Incidentally, as of pdfTEX 1.40.21 (TEX Live 2020), .fmt files are compressed with zlib. This
L2759@P73: makes for a considerable savings in space, and consequently in time.
L2760@P73-74: 74A.6 Testing the installation
L2761@P74: When everything is set up, you can test the installation. A simple test of plain pdfTEX is:

L2774@P74: Variables in texmf.cnf can be overwritten by environment variables. Here are some of the most
L2775@P74: common problems you can encounter when getting started:
L2776@P74: • I can’t find the format file ‘pdftex.fmt’!
L2777@P74: I can’t find the format file ‘pdflatex.fmt’!
L2778@P74: The format file is not created (see above how to do that) or is not properly placed. Make
L2779@P74: sure that TEXFORMATS in texmf.cnf contains the path to pdftex.fmt or pdflatex.fmt.
L2780@P74: • Fatal format file error; I’m stymied
L2781@P74: This typically appears if you forgot to regenerate the .fmt files after installing a new
L2782@P74: version of the pdfTEX binary. The first line tells by which engine the offending format was
L2783@P74: generated.
L2784@P74: • pdfTEX cannot find one or more map files (*.map), encoding vectors (*.enc), virtual fonts,
L2785@P74: Type 1 fonts, TrueType or OpenType fonts, or some image file.
L2786@P74: Make sure that the required file exists and the corresponding variable in texmf.cnf contains a path to the file.
L2787@P74: When you have installed new fonts, and your PDF viewer complains about missing fonts,
L2788@P74: you should take a look at the log file produced by pdfTEX. Missing fonts, map files,
L2789@P74: encoding vectors as well as missing characters (glyphs) are reported there.
